title: German Parliamentary Committee investigation of the NSA spying scandal
text:
In Operation Eikonal German BND agents received "Selector Lists" from the NSA − search terms for their dragnet surveillance. They contain IP addresses, mobile phone numbers and email accounts with the BND surveillance system containing hundreds of thousands and possibly more than a million such targets.[1] These lists have been subject of controversy as in 2008 it was revealed that they contained some terms targeting the European Aeronautic Defence and Space Company (EADS), the Eurocopter project[2] as well as French administration,[3,1] which were first noticed by BND employees in 2005.[2] Other selectors were found to target the administration of Austria.[4] After the revelations made by whistleblower Edward Snowden the BND decided to investigate the issue; in October 2013, this investigation concluded that at least 2,000 of these selectors were aimed at Western European or even German interests, which was a violation of the Memorandum of Agreement that the US and Germany signed in 2002 in the wake of the 9/11 terror attacks.[1] After reports emerged in 2014 that EADS and Eurocopter had been surveillance targets the Left Party and the Greens filed an official request to obtain evidence of the violations.[1,5]

The investigative Parliamentary Committee was set up in spring 2014 and reviewed the selectors and discovered 40,000 suspicious search parameters, including espionage targets in Western European governments and numerous companies. The group also confirmed suspicions that the NSA had systematically violated German interests and concluded that the Americans could have perpetrated economic espionage directly under the Germans' noses.[1,6] The investigative parliamentary committee was not granted access to the NSA's selectors list as an appeal led by opposition politicians failed at Germany's top court - instead the ruling coalition appointed an administrative judge, Kurt Graulich, as a "person of trust" who was granted access to the list and briefed the investigative commission on its contents after analyzing the 40,000 parameters.[7,8] In his almost 300-page report,[9] Graulich concluded that European government agencies were targeted to a significant extent, and that the Americans had therefore breached its agreement with Germany. He also found that German targets subject to special protection from surveillance by domestic intelligence agencies under Germany's Basic Law (Grundgesetz) − including numerous enterprises based in Germany − featured abundantly in the NSA's wishlist.[10] On a different scale, Graulich found that problematic BND-internal selectors had been used until the end of 2013: around two thirds of 3300 targets were related to EU and NATO states.[11,12,13] Klaus Landefeld, a member of the board at the Internet industry association Eco International, met intelligence officials and legislators to present suggestions for improvement, such as streamlining the selector system.[14]
